title: Plan a manageable first trip
text: Choose a campsite and activities that fit everyone’s experience and ability. Consider the season, access on foot or by car, and trip length when packing. Leave your route, departure details, expected return, and park emergency contact with someone staying home. Prepare an alternative plan if conditions make your original trip unsuitable. Practice with unfamiliar equipment before leaving.

title: Check your destination before leaving
text: Before departure, check the land manager’s current information for permits, group limits, site conditions, food storage, pet rules, and fire restrictions. Plan cooking equipment around the rules that apply to your campsite. Be willing to change plans when conditions warrant. title: Start with the essential gear categories
text: Use a packing checklist that covers navigation, sun protection, extra clothing, lighting, first-aid supplies, fire-starting supplies where permitted, repair tools, extra food, water and treatment supplies, and emergency shelter. Adapt it to your activity and conditions; it is a starting point, not a complete equipment list. Pack a headlamp and spare batteries, plus layers for changing weather.

title: Prepare navigation before losing service
text: Download the maps you will need before leaving internet access, and carry a paper map as a backup. Learn how to use your map, compass, or GPS before the trip. Bring extra power for a phone used for navigation. A navigation plan needs both suitable tools and familiarity with them; a phone alone is not a complete plan.

title: Pack shelter and bedding together
text: Plan for a tent, sleeping pad, and sleeping bag suited to the location and season. A tent’s stated capacity describes sleeping space; account separately for gear or pets. Choose bedding for the conditions and your own needs, and keep dry clothes for bedtime. Check local rules before relying on a hammock or shelter tied to trees.

title: Inspect the tent area in daylight
text: Arrive with enough daylight to inspect and set up your campsite. Look for level ground that is not a low spot where rain can collect. Avoid dead branches overhead, unstable trees, cliff edges, and flood-prone hollows. Keep the tent clear of cooking and fire areas, and place guy lines where people are less likely to trip over them.

title: Keep food away from wildlife
text: Keep food out of your tent and secure it using the storage method required at your campground. Some locations require dedicated food lockers; do not assume a car or ordinary container is sufficient. Collect crumbs, scraps, and packaging promptly, and use the campground’s designated waste facilities. Never feed wildlife, and give animals space instead of approaching them.

title: Plan simple meals and practice cooking
text: Choose meals that need few cooking items; a one-pot meal reduces both carrying and washing up. Dry ingredients can save weight, while packaging that flattens is easier to carry out. Plan how perishable ingredients will stay cold. Try an unfamiliar camping stove before departure so you can identify starting problems or broken parts while still at home.
